summary: An IAB document about protocol designs that add metadata to encrypted flows. It argues that designs sharing metadata only by explicit action at the host are better than designs where middleboxes insert it. It follows RFC 7624, on pervasive attacks.

eli5.summary: If a sealed letter gets sticky notes added by strangers along the way, that can leak secrets. Better to let the sender add notes.

questions: why middleboxes should not insert metadata
why middleboxes should not add metadata
subtitle: Why endpoints should add metadata themselves instead of letting intermediaries do it.

tldr.problem: As communications become encrypted, some actors want to restore metadata (like user identity) that encryption removes. Adding this metadata at intermediaries undermines privacy protections.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC recommends that protocol designers allow endpoints to add metadata end-to-end, with explicit user consent, rather than having middleboxes insert it automatically.
tldr.outcome: This guidance follows RFC 7624 on pervasive surveillance threats and informs modern protocol design, including discussions of schemes like DNS client subnet data.

today: RFC 8165 provides design guidance that is broadly referenced in privacy-conscious protocol design. As the Internet continues to adopt encryption, the tension between metadata minimization and functionality remains relevant, and this RFC's recommendation—that endpoints, not intermediaries, add metadata with user consent—continues to influence protocol development.

sections.title: The Metadata Problem in Encrypted Communication
sections.content:
Encryption protects the contents of messages, but it does not hide the metadata—information about who is communicating with whom. As Internet protocols adopt encryption to defend against pervasive surveillance, a new tension emerges: some actors (such as proxies, DNS middleboxes, or VPN services) want to restore or add metadata to encrypted flows so they can provide services like geolocation-based content tailoring, traffic analysis, or regulatory compliance.

This document, following the threat model in RFC 7624 (Confidentiality in the Face of Pervasive Surveillance), examines the implications of a common design pattern: having intermediary devices insert metadata into communications. It argues that this pattern weakens overall privacy and should be avoided in favor of designs where endpoints add metadata themselves with explicit user approval.
sections.eli5: Encryption hides what you write, but shows who you're talking to. When middlemen add notes about you to your encrypted messages, that leaks private info. It's better to add your own notes inside the sealed message.

sections.title: Data Minimization and Metadata Restoration
sections.content:
Data minimization is a core defense against pervasive surveillance. It limits the amount of information disclosed to only what is absolutely necessary to complete a protocol exchange. For example, when a web request is encrypted with TLS, the plaintext headers that identify the user or reveal the request content are no longer visible to network eavesdroppers.

However, other actors—such as DNS resolvers, HTTP proxies, or VPN providers—may still have access to information that data minimization removed from a specific protocol exchange. If these actors then attach that information as metadata to those protocol exchanges, the confidentiality benefit of data minimization is negated. The user still has their privacy erased, only by a different party.

The spec notes two common examples of this pattern. The Forwarded HTTP Extension (RFC 7239) allows a proxy to add the original requester's IP address to encrypted HTTP requests, revealing geolocation to the origin server. The Client Subnet in DNS Queries (RFC 7871) allows DNS proxies to append the client's network subnet to encrypted DNS queries, enabling location-based DNS responses but also leaking the subnet to DNS resolvers.
sections.eli5: You hide your identity with encryption, but a middleman who knows it can add a label saying who you are. That destroys the secrecy even though the message stayed sealed.

sections.title: The Core Recommendation: Endpoint-Controlled Metadata
sections.content:
The RFC's central recommendation is clear: avoid inserting metadata at intermediary devices unless explicitly approved by the user whose data will be added. Instead, design protocols so that endpoints can add metadata end-to-end, flowing directly from sender to recipient, and only when the user has explicitly consented.

This approach offers two advantages. First, it improves privacy by giving users control over what information leaves their device and when. Second, it ensures consistency: both communicating parties see the same metadata, regardless of what path the traffic takes. An intermediary-inserted value might differ at different times or devices.

The RFC illustrates this using RFC 7871 as an example. Rather than having a DNS proxy add subnet information, a cleaner design would let clients determine their own subnet (using STUN or similar mechanisms), add it to their DNS queries, and send it end-to-end. This would require clients to be upgraded, but it would provide better privacy properties and avoid the intermediary as a trusted party.
sections.eli5: Instead of a middleman adding your info to messages, you put it in yourself when you choose to. Both sides see what you wanted them to know, and you're in control.

sections.title: Why Deployment Sometimes Favors Intermediaries
sections.content:
Despite the privacy advantages of endpoint-controlled metadata, deployment realities often favor intermediate approaches. Three tensions are particularly common.

Speed of deployment is the first. Proxies and middleboxes are under centralized management and can be upgraded quickly, while end-user devices (like browsers) have a long tail of old versions still in service. An intermediary-based solution can provide functionality immediately to all users, while an end-system solution requires waiting for upgrades to propagate widely.

Content tailoring is the second. Some services need metadata to function—for example, content blocking by network origin may be a regulatory requirement in certain jurisdictions. Where functionality depends on metadata, trusting an intermediary is fragile but sometimes unavoidable. Users who don't desire this functionality have little recourse.

Latency is the third. If an endpoint must discover metadata about itself (such as its public IP address) before sending it, that discovery process (like a STUN exchange) adds latency and discourages adoption of host-based solutions.

These tensions do not change the recommendation, but they explain why some protocols have chosen the intermediary path anyway.
sections.eli5: Making a middleman do it is fast and works for everyone immediately. Making endpoints do it takes time to roll out and adds delay for each user to figure out their own info. That's why some take shortcuts.
